newsitem.title: USA: Stocks, bonds rebound after tumbling on strong data.
newsitem.headline: Stocks, bonds rebound after tumbling on strong data.

text.p: Stocks ended little changed Monday as a broad rally in retailing shares rescued the market from a sharp sell-off sparked by strong economic reports.
Bonds ended slightly weaker, after a surge in the dollar helped ease inflation jitters.
The Nasdaq composite index, heavily weighted with the stocks of computer makers and other high-technology companies, set its sixth consecutive record, rising 7.21 to 1,299.82.

"Retailers and the usual list of tech suspects are helping us out. Some retailers are saying it was the best Thanksgiving weekend (for Christmas sales) in history," said Michael LaTronica, director of research at Gruntal & Co.
The Dow Jones industrial average ended at 6,521.70, unchanged from Friday, after falling about 49 points earlier in the session.

In the broader market, 1,270 stocks rose and 1,200 fell on active New York Stock Exchange volume of 412.5 million shares. The market was closed for Thanksgiving on Thursday and held a shortened session on Friday.

Bond prices fell early in the session on surprisingly strong economic data, which fanned investors' worries about inflation and a possible move by the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates. That pressured stocks in early trading, and the Dow was off more than 30 points for much of the morning.
But as bonds rebounded a bit stocks started roaring back.
"The stronger numbers caused bonds to shake out but it's hard to stop the momentum. There's still the affinity to buy," said Larry Wachtel, a market analyst at Prudential Securities.

The National Association of Purchasing Management said its index of manufacturing rose to 52.7 in November from 50.2 in October, compared with forecasts for 50.8. A reading above 50 signals growth while one below that points to contraction.
Separately, the Commerce Department said construction spending rose 1.8 percent in October, suprising analysts who had forecast that spending dropped.
Analysts said that after the Dow's spectacular 8 percent rise in November, the market was due for a pause.
"It was actually a pretty good day because the focus shifted from blue chips, and gave those a rest, to secondaries and other techs," Wachtel said.
In the bond market, the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond weakened 1/32, leaving its yield unchanged at 6.36 percent.
Strong U.S. economic data and supportive comments from a German official sent the dollar to near two-year highs against the German mark, the Swiss franc and the French franc.
The dollar closed at 1.5545 German marks, about one-and-a-half pfennigs better than Friday's close of 1.5390, but slightly down from a 23-month session high of 1.5590.

The dollar surged to close at 1.3215 Swiss francs vs. 1.3043 on Friday, after reaching a 23-month high of 1.3280 earlier. Against the French franc, the dollar ended at 5.2730, after touching a 22-month high of 5.2820 French francs.
The dollar ended the session at 114.55 Japanese yen, up from Friday's close of 113.87.

Strong gasoline prices at the pump during the Thanksgiving holiday weekend and refinery strikes in Europe pushed gasoline futures to contract highs on the New York Mercantile Exchange, which had been closed since Thursday.
NYMEX gasoline for January delivery closed up 2.66 cents at 68.12 cents per gallon.
Gasoline's strength boosted crude oil and heating oil, with January crude oil up $1.05 at $24.80 per barrel and January heating oil up 1.89 cents at 73.57 cents per gallon.
At the New York's Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange, March coffee futures tumbled 1.70 cents to 106.05 cents per pound on speculative selling.
Overseas, London's FTSE 100 index of leading stocks ended 19.5 points lower at 4,038.5. In Tokyo, the Nikkei 225 ended down 345.67 points or 1.64 percent at 20,674.69.
